title: Khema's mirror
hookLine: a commentary story: the proud queen Khema is shown a beautiful woman growing old before her eyes, and understands (Dhammapada 347 story)

lines: AT THE END OF THE PATH.
cards: Some people avoid the doctor because of what the doctor might say. Queen Khema avoided the Buddha for the same reason.

She was the chief queen of King Bimbisara, the Dhammapada commentary says, very beautiful, and very proud of it. She had heard that the Buddha spoke about the faults of the body's beauty, and she didn't want to hear it.
So the king found a gentle way. He had songs made about the loveliness of the Bamboo Grove, the park where the Buddha stayed, until she wanted to see it for herself. She went to see the gardens.
And at the end of the path, there he was.

teach.h: A WOMAN MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN HER.
teach.b: First, the vision. The commentary says that as Khema approached, the Buddha caused her to see a young woman standing beside him, fanning him, more beautiful than Khema herself. And Khema thought: next to her, I'm nothing.
Second, the change. As she watches, the young woman grows older: youth into middle age, middle age into old age, gray hair, broken teeth, wrinkled skin. Then she falls, and lies still.
What takes a lifetime takes moments.

This is Khema's mirror: not glass, but a face she envied, showing her what every face will do, her own included. Third, the verse. The commentary places Dhammapada verse three hundred forty-seven here.
In Max Muller's old translation it says that those who are slaves to passions run down with the stream, "as a spider runs down the web which he has made himself." Notice where the trouble is.
Beauty isn't the enemy in this story. The web is the clinging, and she spun it herself. Fourth, what she did with it.
The commentary says Khema understood right there, still wearing her royal ornaments, and with the king's blessing she went forth as a nun.
The Anguttara Nikaya names Khema foremost among the nuns in wisdom.
The queen who stayed away so she wouldn't hear about aging became a nun remembered for her wisdom.

how: Khema's story is told with Dhammapada verse 347 in Theravada teaching, and reflection on the body's aging is a traditional practice for loosening attachment, taught with care not to turn it into self-dislike.

o: a reflecting pool in the Bamboo Grove
a jeweled mirror the queen gave the monks
a vision of beauty aging, which freed a queen

p: a young woman who grows old
a spider and its own web

s: Khema went to hear the Buddha as soon as she could
she stayed away, afraid of what he would say about beauty, until songs about the garden drew her.
in the verse, the web is something the spider makes itself
"as a spider runs down the web which he has made himself".
the story teaches that beauty is bad
the trouble is the clinging, the web; Khema saw that beauty ages and let go.

games.q: you're Khema. you hear the Buddha speaks about the faults of the body's beauty. what do you do?
games.why: she stays away, until the king's songs about the Bamboo Grove draw her there, and the vision of a woman aging changes everything.

practice: Use a mirror or a phone camera if one is nearby, or picture your face in your mind, and look at it the way you'd look at someone you love who is getting older: a line by the eyes, a gray hair, or the place where one will be.
Don't judge it, and don't fix it; just notice it's changing, as Khema saw, and let the looking stay warm. Then close your eyes, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Khema's mirror. A vision of a beautiful woman growing old, which showed a proud queen the web she'd spun herself. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Khema: her name, which means safety, security.

carryVoice: Your line: beauty ages. She saw it, and was free of the web. Rest well.
